pamphlet_excerpts: Three- to Five-minute Introduction: Give A Three- to Five-minute: You Are a Public Speaker (p. 7).
Three- to Five-minute Introduction Principle 2: Give A Three- to Five-minute Principle 2: Poking a little fun at yourself is another way to score points with audiences (p. 7).

Three- to Five-minute Introduction Principle 3: Give A Three- to Five-minute Principle 3: The speech seeks to make the audience believe or accept your point of view, or stimulate or inspire your audience (p. 7).
Three- to Five-minute Introduction Principle 4: Give A Three- to Five-minute Principle 4: For instance, let's say you live in an urban neighborhood (p. 7).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Three- to Five-minute Introduction): Step 1 (Give A Three- to Five-minute): Your city council wants to turn your only neighborhood basketball court into a much-needed parking lot (p. 7).
Step 2 (Three- to Five-minute Introduction): Step 2 (Give A Three- to Five-minute): You decide to give a speech to your class about how much the basketball court means to you and your friends (p. 7).

Step 3 (Three- to Five-minute Introduction): Step 3 (Give A Three- to Five-minute): Your goal is to call attention to this issue and inspire the audience to care about the basketball court as much (p. 7).

Step 4 (Three- to Five-minute Introduction): Step 4 (Give A Three- to Five-minute): Cite the lack of playground facilities in your area, or how many students who once played at the local court went on to play high school and/or (p. 7).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When delivering an introduction or short speech to an audience, how should you use your notes, eye contact, and vocal delivery?
quiz_item.question: When delivering an introduction or short speech to an audience, how should you use your notes, eye contact, and vocal delivery?
options: A. Read your speech word-for-word from a full sheet of paper held in front of your face while speaking as rapidly as possible.
B. Stare at a single spot on the back wall above the audience's heads and speak in a flat monotone to avoid sounding nervous.
C. Use brief keyword outline notes to stay organized while maintaining natural eye contact across the audience, projecting your voice clearly, and varying your pace and pitch.
D. Pace continuously back and forth across the stage while looking down at the floor to remember memorized sentences.
choices: A. Read your speech word-for-word from a full sheet of paper held in front of your face while speaking as rapidly as possible.
B. Stare at a single spot on the back wall above the audience's heads and speak in a flat monotone to avoid sounding nervous.
C. Use brief keyword outline notes to stay organized while maintaining natural eye contact across the audience, projecting your voice clearly, and varying your pace and pitch.
D. Pace continuously back and forth across the stage while looking down at the floor to remember memorized sentences.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Use brief keyword outline notes to stay organized while maintaining natural eye contact across the audience, projecting your voice clearly, and varying your pace and pitch.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Effective public speaking engages listeners through an organized opening, body, and conclusion delivered conversationally from keyword notes with steady eye contact and clear vocal projection.

Impromptu Talk Principle 4: Give An Impromptu Talk Principle 4: Suppose you are at a Scout meeting and the Scoutmaster asks you, without warning, to tell the troop about plans foran upcoming campout to Three Rivers State (p. 43).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Impromptu Talk): Step 1 (Give An Impromptu Talk): Think for a moment what you know about the campout, then quickly organize your thoughts (p. 43).
Step 2 (Impromptu Talk): Step 2 (Give An Impromptu Talk): Don't be afraid to pause for a second and reflect on the question or topic you have been asked to present (p. 43).
Step 3 (Impromptu Talk): Step 3 (Give An Impromptu Talk): Remind Scouts at the end of your speech to check with their folks about volunteering as chaperones (p. 43).
Step 4 (Impromptu Talk): Step 4 (Give An Impromptu Talk): You probablywon't be asked to talk about a topic you don't know something about (p. 43).

pamphlet_excerpts: Topic of Interest: Select a topic of interest: Now that you have prepared your speech and practiced in front of friends and family, you are ready to deliver your speech to the intended audience (p. 31).
Topic of Interest Principle 2: Select a topic of interest Principle 2: Your first task is to prepare the room where you plan to speak (p. 31).
Topic of Interest Principle 3: Select a topic of interest Principle 3: If your equipment uses electrical outlets, be prepared (p. 31).
Topic of Interest Principle 4: Select a topic of interest Principle 4: Bring a three-prong/two-prong outlet adapter and an extension cord (p. 31).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Topic of Interest): Step 1 (Select a topic of interest): Also bring a small flashlight or penlight in case you have to darken the room and still need to refer to your notes (p. 31).

pamphlet_excerpts: You know parliamentary procedure by leading: Come to Order, Parliamentary Procedure Made Easy In formal meetings, the chair, or leader, conducts all business (p. 45).
You know parliamentary procedure by leading Principle 2: While the leader of an informal meeting may participate in the discussion, the chair of a formal meeting only conducts the meeting (p. 45).
You know parliamentary procedure by leading Principle 3: Speakers must be recognized by the chair and technically, all remarks are directed to the chair (p. 45).
You know parliamentary procedure by leading Principle 4: Questions from individual to individual also are directed via the chair (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (You know parliamentary procedure by leading): The formal meeting is more a debate of opposing ideas, each of which strives for audience approval (p. 45).

Step 2 (You know parliamentary procedure by leading): The chair enforces the rules equally on all participants to ensure that each person has a fair opportunity to present his or her point of view (p. 45).
Step 3 (You know parliamentary procedure by leading): Responsibility for keeping the meeting going also means keeping it focused (p. 45).

Step 4 (You know parliamentary procedure by leading): When the discussion While informal discussions do not have rules, the chair must apply common sense ideas for a successful meeting to take place (p. 45).
